==Type 1 diabetes== (T1D) removes the body's main source of endogenous insulin. That change affects much more than a single glucose-lowering signal: it alters hepatic glucose regulation, peripheral glucose uptake, counterregulation, meal timing, exercise responses, and the relationship between an insulin dose and its later effect. A serious game that represents these processes needs enough of this structure to produce understandable causal patterns without implying that a simplified system can predict an individual person's response.

This module is relevant when gameplay makes claims about glucose trajectories, insulin action, meals, exercise, treatment decisions, or other physiological consequences. It is not a universal requirement for every T1D game. A psychosocial, narrative, communication, procedural, or empathy-oriented game may not require a glucose–insulin model; it instead requires evidence and domain review appropriate to the constructs and experiences it represents.

This module is a scientific orientation for developers, researchers, writers, and evaluators. It separates three kinds of statement throughout:

- **Established evidence** describes mechanisms or recurring clinical patterns supported by human physiology and T1D studies.
- **Evidence limitations** identify population, protocol, measurement, or transferability constraints.
- **Modelling and design inference** translates evidence into possible educational representations. These inferences are design choices, not clinical findings.

## Module map

1. [The glucose–insulin system](glucose-insulin-system.qmd) explains glucose sources, tissue uptake, insulin action, hepatic regulation, counterregulation, and measurement lag.
2. [Meals, insulin, and exercise](meals-insulin-exercise.qmd) focuses on interacting time courses: nutrient appearance, subcutaneous insulin action, aerobic activity, and high-intensity or resistance activity.
3. [Variability and safety](variability-and-safety.qmd) covers circadian effects, illness, sleep, stress, alcohol, temperature, injection-site variability, hypoglycaemia, ketosis, and educational boundaries.
4. [Model families](model-families.qmd) compares major glucose–insulin model families and explains how purpose, identifiability, transparency, and validation constrain their use in games.

## The minimum causal picture

An educational representation of T1D should preserve four ideas.

First, glucose concentration reflects competing fluxes rather than a moral score or a direct measure of effort. Meals and endogenous production add glucose; tissues consume or store it; the kidneys can excrete glucose at sufficiently high concentrations. The balance changes continuously ([Petersen et al., 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28731034/); [Gerich, 2010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20546255/)).

Second, exogenous insulin is delayed and variable because it must leave a subcutaneous depot before reaching the circulation. Its timing cannot reproduce the rapid, portal delivery of endogenous insulin, and identical nominal doses need not create identical action profiles ([Heinemann, 2002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12450450/); [Najjar and Perdomo, 2019](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30968756/)).

Third, context matters. Exercise can increase muscle glucose uptake independently of insulin and can increase insulin sensitivity after activity; illness and some forms of intense exercise can increase hepatic glucose output; sleep, circadian phase, stress, temperature, and tissue condition can modify the response ([Sylow et al., 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27739515/); [Riddell et al., 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28126459/)).

Fourth, short-term glucose outcomes are uncertain even when the direction of a mechanism is known. Between-person variability, within-person day-to-day variability, imperfect sensing, unobserved context, and model-form error all contribute. A game should therefore teach conditional reasoning and pattern recognition rather than present a single trajectory as biologically inevitable.

## Design principles derived from the evidence

::: {.callout-note title="Modelling and design inference"}
These are development principles inferred from the science, not treatment recommendations.

1. Represent **delays and overlap**. Meals, insulin, exercise, and counterregulatory responses unfold on different time scales.
2. Expose **state dependence**. The same action can have a different outcome when active insulin, meal absorption, recent exercise, illness, or time of day differs.
3. Preserve **directional asymmetry**. Moderate aerobic exercise commonly lowers glucose when insulin is active; intense exercise can transiently raise it through catecholamine-driven hepatic output.
4. Include **bounded variability**. Variation should be interpretable and linked to visible or teachable causes where possible, not added as unexplained randomness.
5. Treat adverse events as **safety concepts**, not punishment. Explanations should be factual, calm, and paired with clear educational signposting.
6. Keep simulation distinct from care. Do not convert game outcomes into personal dose advice, diagnosis, or emergency guidance.
:::

## Scope

Included here are short-horizon glucose physiology, subcutaneous insulin action, meals, activity, selected contextual modifiers, acute safety concepts, and general model-family comparisons. Detailed immunology, prevention, long-term complications, device procurement, cost-effectiveness, and individual treatment algorithms are outside this module. Population findings are not presented as personal predictions.
